lesson.title: The Term That Runs the Show
lesson.summary: Inside any polynomial, one term eventually overwhelms all the others as x grows large, and identifying that dominant term is the shortcut to predicting end behavior without graphing anything.
lesson.body:
A polynomial such as p(x) = a_n x^n + a_(n-1) x^(n-1) + ... + a_1 x + a_0 is a sum of terms of different degrees, and comparing growth rates term by term shows that the highest-degree term, a_n x^n, eventually dominates every other term combined. This follows directly from growth rate comparison: since x^n grows faster than x^m whenever n is greater than m, the ratio of any lower-degree term to the leading term shrinks toward 0 as x grows without bound. The leading term is therefore called the dominant term, and for describing what happens as x approaches positive or negative infinity, the rest of the polynomial can essentially be ignored.

More precisely, p(x) divided by its dominant term a_n x^n approaches 1 as x approaches infinity, because every other term divided by a_n x^n approaches 0. This means p(x) behaves more and more like the single power function a_n x^n as x grows large, even though the two are not equal for any finite x.

Consider p(x) = 2x^3 - 5x^2 + 1, whose dominant term is 2x^3. Evaluate both at x=100: p(100) = 2(1,000,000) - 5(10,000) + 1 = 2,000,000 - 50,000 + 1 = 1,950,001, while the dominant term alone gives 2(100)^3 = 2,000,000. The ratio 1,950,001/2,000,000 is 0.975, already close to 1. Push to x=1000: p(1000) = 2(1,000,000,000) - 5(1,000,000) + 1 = 2,000,000,000 - 5,000,000 + 1 = 1,995,000,001, while the dominant term gives 2(1000)^3 = 2,000,000,000. The ratio is now 1,995,000,001/2,000,000,000 = 0.9975, even closer to 1. The lower-degree terms are still present and still nonzero, but their share of the total keeps shrinking as x grows.

The same reasoning applies with a negative leading coefficient, just with the sign flipped throughout. For p(x) = -x^4 + 3x - 1, the dominant term is -x^4, which is negative and unbounded in size for both large positive and large negative x, since x^4 is always positive regardless of the sign of x. At x=10, p(10) = -10,000 + 30 - 1 = -9,971, while the dominant term alone gives -10,000; the ratio -9,971/-10,000 is 0.9971, again close to 1. Because the dominant term is negative and has even degree, both ends of this polynomial's graph point downward toward negative infinity, exactly the opposite of a positive even-degree leading term.

The dominant term controls two separate features of a polynomial's end behavior: its overall size and its sign. Because 2x^3 becomes arbitrarily large and positive as x approaches infinity, so does p(x); because 2x^3 becomes arbitrarily large and negative as x approaches negative infinity (an odd power of a negative number stays negative), so does p(x). This is exactly the leading coefficient test used to sketch polynomial graphs: an even degree with positive leading coefficient sends both ends upward, an odd degree with positive leading coefficient sends the left end down and the right end up, and flipping the sign of the leading coefficient flips both ends.

Identifying the dominant term is also the first step in analyzing rational functions, where the end behavior of the numerator's dominant term compared to the denominator's dominant term determines whether the function settles onto a horizontal line, a slanted line, or grows without bound, exactly the topic of the next section.
